claim: TAPBPR performs peptide editing on major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC I) molecules
source: Tapasin and TAPBPR are known to perform peptide editing on major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC I) molecules
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about TAPBPR function

claim: The K22-D35 loop of TAPBPR plays a critical role in mediating peptide exchange on MHC I
source: we reveal a critical role for the K22-D35 loop of TAPBPR in mediating peptide exchange on MHC I
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript

claim: A specific leucine within the K22-D35 loop enables TAPBPR to facilitate peptide dissociation from MHC I
source: We identify a specific leucine within this loop that enables TAPBPR to facilitate peptide dissociation from MHC I
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated through mutagenesis experiments

claim: Chaperone-mediated peptide editing on MHC I can occur by different mechanisms dependent on the C-terminal residue that the MHC I accommodates in its F pocket
source: These data reveal that chaperone-mediated peptide editing on MHC I can occur by different mechanisms dependent on the C-terminal residue that the MHC I accommodates in its F pocket
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the abstract based on the experimental findings

claim: MHC I molecules play a critical role in immunosurveillance by presenting antigenic peptides to CD8+ T cells
source: Major histocompatibility complex class I (MHC I) molecules play a critical role in immmunosurveillance, particularly in the context of viral infections and cancer, by presenting antigenic peptides to CD8 +T cells
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about MHC I function

claim: MHC I molecules undergo peptide editing prior to their cell surface export
source: Prior to their cell surface export, MHC I molecules undergo peptide editing, a process that involves the exchange of low-affinity peptides for those of higher affinity
evidence: This is established knowledge about MHC I processing

claim: Peptide editing ensures that only stable peptide:MHC I complexes are released to the plasma membrane
source: In addition to ensuring that only stable peptide:MHC I complexes are released to the plasma membrane, peptide editing ultimately controls the peptide repertoire that is displayed for immune detection
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of peptide editing

claim: Tapasin was the only known peptide editor for MHC I for over two decades
source: For over two decades, tapasin was the only known peptide editor for MHC I, facilitating peptide selection within the confines of the peptide loading complex (PLC) (Williams et al., 2002; Howarth et al., 2004; Chen and Bouvier, 2007; Wearsch and Cresswell, 2007)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: TAPBPR is a second independent peptide editor that performs peptide exchange outside the PLC
source: However, it is now well-recognised that the tapasin-related protein TAPBPR is a second independent peptide editor that performs peptide exchange outside the PLC (Boyle et al., 2013; Hermann et al., 2013; Hermann et al., 2015; Morozov et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: TAPBPR can work in cooperation with UGT1 to reglucosylate MHC I, causing recycling of MHC molecules to the PLC
source: Furthermore, TAPBPR can work in cooperation with UDP-glucose:glycoprotein glucosyltransferase 1 (UGT1) to reglucosylate MHC I, causing recycling of MHC molecules to the PLC (Neerincx et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work

claim: When given access to surface expressed MHC I molecules, TAPBPR retains its function as a peptide exchange catalyst
source: Although TAPBPR usually functions as an intracellular peptide editor, we have recently made the fascinating discovery that when given access to surface expressed MHC I molecules, TAPBPR retains its function as a peptide exchange catalyst and can be utilised to display immunogenic peptides of choice directly onto the surface of cells (Ilca et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors

claim: The crystal structures of human TAPBPR in complex with mouse MHC I captured the endpoint of peptide editing
source: The recently reported crystal structures of human TAPBPR in complex with mouse MHC I captured the endpoint of peptide editing, thereby suggesting that TAPBPR facilitates peptide exchange by widening the peptide binding groove of MHC I at the α2–1 region (Jiang et al., 2017; Thomas and Tampé, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to the crystal structure papers

claim: There is an incomplete understanding of the step-by-step processes by which TAPBPR and tapasin recognize peptide-loaded MHC I molecules and facilitate peptide dissociation
source: However, there remains an incomplete understanding of the step-by-step processes by which the two peptide editors, TAPBPR and tapasin, recognise peptide-loaded MHC I molecules and actively facilitate peptide dissociation to result in the conformations observed in the crystal structures
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field

claim: The structure reported by Thomas and Tampe identified a loop of TAPBPR that was proposed to interact with the peptide binding groove of MHC I
source: Intriguingly, the structure reported by Thomas and Tampe identified a loop of TAPBPR that was proposed to interact with the peptide binding groove of MHC I, where the C-terminus of bound peptide usually resides (Thomas and Tampé, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the Thomas and Tampe structure paper

claim: There is no experimental evidence to support that the TAPBPR loop mediates peptide exchange on MHC I
source: While this study demonstrated the localisation of the loop, to date, there is no experimental evidence to support the notion that this loop mediates peptide exchange on MHC I
evidence: This is a statement about the lack of functional evidence in the literature

claim: Jiang et al. failed to capture the loop in proximity to the peptide-binding groove
source: In contrast, Jiang et al. failed to capture the loop in proximity to the peptide-binding groove (Jiang et al., 2017), further questioning the relevance and importance of this loop in TAPBPR-mediated peptide exchange
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the Jiang et al. structure paper

claim: The TAPBPR loop region lies close to the peptide binding groove of MHC I, in the proximity of the F pocket
source: Our docking identified a region of TAPBPR that lies close to the peptide binding groove of MHC I, in the proximity of the F pocket (Figure 1a, dotted circle)
evidence: This is based on computational docking studies performed by the authors

claim: The loop region differs between tapasin and TAPBPR
source: This region contained a loop that differs between tapasin and TAPBPR
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison

claim: In tapasin, the loop appears to be rather short and is not sufficiently well ordered in the crystal structure to be visible
source: In tapasin, this loop appears to be rather short and is not sufficiently well ordered in the crystal structure to be visible (Dong et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the tapasin structure

claim: In TAPBPR, the loop is significantly longer than in tapasin
source: while in TAPBPR this loop is significantly longer (Figure 1b)
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison shown in the figure

claim: The two crystal structures of the TAPBPR-MHC I complex support the prediction that the loop region is very near the F pocket
source: The two crystal structures of the TAPBPR-MHC I complex support our prediction regarding the arrangement of TAPBPR relative to MHC I, including this loop region being very near the F pocket (Figure 1c)
evidence: This is based on comparison with published crystal structures

claim: The position and orientation of the loop in the crystal structures is poorly defined
source: However, the position and orientation of the loop in the structures is poorly defined
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure data

claim: In the structure from Jiang et al. (2017), the loop is not sufficiently well ordered to be modelled
source: In the structure from Jiang et al. (2017), this loop is not sufficiently well ordered to be modelled
evidence: This is based on analysis of the published crystal structure

claim: In the structure from Thomas and Tampé (2017), several side chains and backbone atoms of the loop do not fit the electron density well
source: In the structure from Thomas and Tampé (2017), the loop has been modelled; however, the electron density into which it was built is not well defined: several side chains and even several of the backbone atoms do not fit the electron density well (Figure 1d)
evidence: This is based on analysis of the electron density map from the published structure

claim: All TAPBPR loop mutants are stably expressed at similar levels to TAPBPRWT
source: steady state expression of all the TAPBPR loop mutants was similar to TAPBPRWT
evidence: This is demonstrated by western blotting shown in Figure 1e

claim: All TAPBPR loop variants interact equally well with both MHC I and UGT1
source: all variants interacted equally well with both MHC I and UGT1 (Figure 1e)
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1e

claim: The overall protein stability and structure of TAPBPR was not significantly affected by changes to the loop
source: suggesting the overall protein stability and structure of TAPBPR was not significantly affected by the changes to the loop
evidence: This is inferred from the expression and interaction data

claim: Plasma membrane expressed TAPBPRØloop enhanced the binding of an exogenous fluorescent peptide specific for HLA-A*68:02 to a similar extent as TAPBPRWT
source: When exploring the ability of TAPBPR to promote peptide association, we found plasma membrane expressed TAPBPRØloop enhanced the binding of an exogenous fluorescent peptide specific for HLA-A*68:02 (YVVPFVAK*V) onto cells to a similar extent as TAPBPRWT (Figure 2a)
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2a

claim: TAPBPRØloop is unable to efficiently mediate peptide dissociation from HLA-A*68:02
source: when we tested the ability of TAPBPR to mediate peptide dissociation (i.e. removal of the bound fluorescent peptide in the presence of an unlabelled competitor peptide) (Figure 2b), in contrast to the efficient exchange observed with TAPBPRWT, very little, if any, dissociation of fluorescent peptide was observed with TAPBPRØloop (Figure 2c–2e)
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide exchange assays shown in Figures 2c-2e

claim: The K22-D35 loop of TAPBPR is essential for mediating efficient peptide dissociation from HLA-A*68:02
source: This suggests that the K22-D35 loop of TAPBPR is essential for mediating efficient peptide dissociation from HLA-A*68:02
evidence: This is concluded from the peptide exchange assay data

claim: TAPBPRL30G is incapable of mediating efficient peptide dissociation from HLA-A*68:02
source: when we explored the ability of TAPBPRL30G to mediate fluorescent peptide dissociation from HLA-A*68:02, we found that it was incapable of mediating efficient peptide dissociation in the presence of unlabelled competitor (Figure 2c–2e)
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide exchange assays shown in Figures 2c-2e

claim: Alteration of the single leucine residue (L30) had the same effect on TAPBPR function as mutating the entire loop
source: Strikingly, alteration of this single residue had the same effect on the function of TAPBPR as mutating the entire loop
evidence: This is concluded from comparing the functional data for L30G and Øloop mutants

claim: TAPBPRØG30L, in which the leucine residue alone is restored into the dysfunctional TAPBPRØloop molecule, transforms it into a functioning peptide exchange catalyst on HLA-A*68:02
source: The crucial role of L30 in mediating peptide dissociation was further supported with our observation that TAPBPRØG30L, in which the leucine residue alone is restored into the dysfunctional TAPBPRØloop molecule, transformed it into a functioning peptide exchange catalyst on HLA-A*68:02, albeit at reduced capability compared to TAPBPRWT (Figure 2c–2e)
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide exchange assays shown in Figures 2c-2e

claim: L30 is a critical residue within the loop of TAPBPR for mediating peptide dissociation from HLA-A*68:02
source: These results suggest that L30 is a critical residue within the loop of TAPBPR for mediating peptide dissociation from HLA-A*68:02
evidence: This is concluded from the mutagenesis and functional data

claim: Soluble TAPBPR can efficiently promote peptide exchange on HLA-A*68:02, HLA-A2 and H-2Kb
source: We have also recently shown that soluble TAPBPR, consisting only of the lumenal domains of the wild-type molecule (i.e. lacking its transmembrane region and cytoplasmic tail) can also efficiently promote peptide exchange on three MHC I molecules: HLA-A*68:02, HLA-A2 and H-2Kb (Ilca et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work

claim: All TAPBPR loop variants have a similar melting temperature as TAPBPRWT
source: Differential scanning fluorimetry revealed all TAPBPR loop variants had a similar melting temperature as TAPBPRWT (Figure 3b)
evidence: This is demonstrated by differential scanning fluorimetry data shown in Figure 3b

claim: The alterations made to the loop had not significantly affected protein folding and stability
source: indicating the alterations made to the loop had not significantly affected protein folding and stability
evidence: This is inferred from the melting temperature data

claim: TAPBPRWT is the most efficient at mediating peptide exchange on HLA-A*68:02, followed by TAPBPRØG30L
source: Comparison of the ability of the soluble TAPBPR variants to mediate peptide exchange on HLA-A*68:02 molecules on HeLaM cells revealed that TAPBPRWT was most efficient, followed by TAPBPRØG30L, which exhibited ~33% peptide exchange activity relative to TAPBPRWT (in the presence of 10 nM ETVSK*QSNV) (Figure 3c and d)
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide exchange assays shown in Figures 3c and 3d

claim: Both TAPBPRL30G and TAPBPRØloop display only ~3% of the exchange activity of TAPBPRWT
source: However, both TAPBPRL30G and TAPBPRØloop were unable to efficiently mediating peptide exchange, displaying only ~3% of the exchange activity of TAPBPRWT (in the presence of 10 nM ETVSK*QSNV) (Figure 3c and d)
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide exchange assays shown in Figures 3c and 3d

claim: Soluble TAPBPRTN5 did not mediate any peptide exchange
source: As previously shown (Ilca et al., 2018), soluble TAPBPRTN5, a mutant which cannot bind to MHC I, did not mediate any peptide exchange (Figure 3c and d)
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide exchange assays and supported by a citation

claim: The hierarchy of peptide exchange efficiency (WT>ØG30L>L30G>TN5) was maintained over a wide range of exogenous TAPBPR concentrations
source: This hierarchy (WT>ØG30L>L30G>TN5) was maintained over a wide range of exogenous TAPBPR concentrations (Figure 3e)
evidence: This is demonstrated by dose-response curves shown in Figure 3e

claim: TAPBPRWT is the most efficient binder to HLA-A*68:02, followed by TAPBPRØG30L
source: When we determined the ability of the soluble TAPBPR variants to bind to HLA-A*68:02, TAPBPRWT was the most efficient binder, followed by TAPBPRØG30L (Figure 4a)
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry binding assays shown in Figure 4a

claim: TAPBPRL30G and TAPBPRØloop are unable to make productive interactions with surface expressed HLA-A*68:02
source: However, TAPBPRL30G and TAPBPRØloop were unable to make productive interactions with surface expressed HLA-A*68:02 (Figure 4a)
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry binding assays shown in Figure 4a

claim: All soluble TAPBPR variants (with the exception of TAPBPRTN5) are capable of binding significant amounts of MHC I from cell lysates
source: All soluble TAPBPR variants (with the exception of TAPBPRTN5) were capable of binding significant amounts of MHC I, although less MHC I was detected bound to TAPBPRL30G and TAPBPRØloop (Figure 4b)
evidence: This is demonstrated by pull-down experiments shown in Figure 4b

claim: TAPBPR molecules with alterations to the loop are able to bind to peptide-receptive MHC I but are unable to physically make MHC I peptide-deficient due to their inability to dissociate peptide
source: Therefore, we speculated that TAPBPR molecules with alterations to the loop are still able to bind to peptide-receptive MHC I but are unable to physically make MHC I peptide-deficient due to their inability to dissociate peptide
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the differential binding to surface vs. lysate MHC I

claim: Incubation of cells at 26°C increases the expression of peptide-receptive MHC I on the plasma membrane
source: Consistent with this, incubation of cells at 26°C, which increases the expression of peptide-receptive MHC I on the plasma membrane (Ljunggren et al., 1990; Schumacher et al., 1990; Garstka et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature

claim: TAPBPR loop variants exhibit increased binding to cells at 26°C compared to 37°C
source: resulted in the TAPBPR loop variants, but not TAPBPRWT, exhibiting increased binding to cells (Compare Figure 4c with Figure 4a summarised in Figure 4d)
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry binding assays at different temperatures

claim: A ~7 fold increase in binding of TAPBPRL30G and TAPBPRØloop was observed at 26°C compared to 37°C
source: While no significant change was observed in the ability of exogenous TAPBPRWT to bind to cells incubated at the lower temperature, a ~ 7 fold increase in binding of TAPBPRL30G and TAPBPRØloop was observed at 26°C compared to 37°C, and the binding of TAPBPRØG30L increased by ~2.5 fold (Figure 4d)
evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of binding data shown in Figure 4d

claim: All soluble TAPBPR variants exhibit a corresponding increase in the ability to mediate peptide exchange when given access to surface expressed peptide-receptive MHC I at 26°C
source: When given access to surface expressed peptide-receptive MHC I upon incubation at 26°C, all soluble TAPBPR variants exhibited a corresponding increase in the ability to mediate peptide exchange (compare Figure 3c (37°C) with Figure 4e (26°C), summarised in Figure 4f)
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide exchange assays at different temperatures

claim: TAPBPR variants lacking L30 are able to bind to peptide-receptive MHC I but are unable to physically make MHC I peptide-deficient due to their inability to efficiently facilitate peptide dissociation
source: These findings suggest that TAPBPR variants lacking L30 are indeed able to bind to peptide-receptive MHC I but are unable to physically make MHC I peptide-deficient due to their inability to efficiently facilitate peptide dissociation
evidence: This is concluded from the temperature-dependent binding and exchange data

claim: There are significant changes in the peptides presented on MHC I upon mutation of the TAPBPR loop
source: When we compared the immunopeptidomes of IFNγ-treated HeLaM-TAPBPRKO cells expressing TAPBPRWT with cells expressing TAPBPRØloop, we found significant changes in the peptides presented on MHC I (Figure 5a)
evidence: This is demonstrated by mass spectrometry immunopeptidomics data shown in Figure 5

claim: 461 peptides were found exclusively in the TAPBPRWT-expressing cells and 550 peptides were found exclusively in the cells expressing the Øloop variant
source: 461 peptides were found exclusively in the TAPBPRWT-expressing cells and 550 peptides were found exclusively in the cells expressing the Øloop variant (Figure 5a)
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunopeptidomics data shown in Figure 5a

claim: 193 peptides exhibit increased abundance in cells expressing TAPBPRWT and 222 peptides display increased abundance in TAPBPRØloop-expressing cells
source: Label-free quantitation by mass spectrometry revealed that there were also significant changes in the abundance of some peptides between TAPBPRWT and TAPBPRØloop, with 193 peptides exhibiting increased abundance in cells expressing TAPBPRWT (Red circles, Figure 5b) and 222 peptides displaying increased abundance in TAPBPRØloop-expressing cells (Blue circles, Figure 5b)
evidence: This is demonstrated by label-free quantitation data shown in Figure 5b

claim: The loop is involved in selecting MHC I peptides within cells
source: Taken together, this data demonstrates that the loop is involved in selecting MHC I peptides within cells and highlights the importance of leucine 30 in the peptide selection process, particularly for HLA-A*68:02 molecules
evidence: This is concluded from the immunopeptidomics data

claim: TAPBPR with a functional loop is preferentially stripping a proportion of peptides from HLA-A*68:02 molecules, but not from the HLA-B or -C molecules found on HeLaM cells
source: This suggests that TAPBPR with a functional loop is preferentially stripping a proportion of peptides from HLA-A*68:02 molecules, but not from the HLA-B or -C molecules found on HeLaM cells
evidence: This is concluded from the immunopeptidomics data showing differential effects on HLA-A*68:02 vs. other HLA molecules

claim: Soluble TAPBPRWT exhibits a strong interaction with HLA-A*68:02
source: To explore this further, we compared the ability of soluble TAPBPR to bind to soluble heterotrimeric HLA-A*68:02, -B*15:03 or -C*12:03 molecules coupled to beads. This revealed a strong interaction between TAPBPRWT and HLA-A*68:02 (Figure 5—source data 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by binding assays to bead-coupled MHC I molecules

claim: Soluble TAPBPRWT fails to bind to heterotrimeric HLA-B*15:03 and –C*12:03 molecules
source: However, soluble TAPBPRWT failed to bind to heterotrimeric HLA-B*15:03 and –C*12:03 molecules (Figure 5—source data 1)
evidence: This is demonstrated by binding assays to bead-coupled MHC I molecules

claim: HLA-A*68:02 accommodates an aliphatic residue in its F pocket
source: Hence, while both molecules have a similar anchor residue in their B pocket, the F pocket of HLA-A*68:02 accommodates an aliphatic residue
evidence: This is based on known peptide binding motifs and supported by a citation

claim: HLA-A*68:01 accommodates a basic residue in its F pocket
source: whereas the F pocket of HLA-A*68:01 accommodates a basic residue (Figure 6a) (Niu et al., 2013)
evidence: This is based on known peptide binding motifs and supported by a citation

claim: HLA-A*02:01 accommodates very similar anchor residues in both B and F pockets as HLA-A*68:02
source: Compared to HLA-A*68:02, HLA-A*02:01 accommodates very similar anchor residues in both B and F pockets
evidence: This is based on known peptide binding motifs

claim: H-2Kb has a completely different binding motif from HLA-A*68:02, with the exception that it binds a similar anchor residue in the F pocket
source: whereas H-2Kb has a completely different binding motif, with the exception that it binds a similar anchor residue in the F pocket (Figure 6a)
evidence: This is based on known peptide binding motifs

claim: TAPBPRWT is the most efficient catalyst on both HLA-A*02:01 and H-2Kb, followed by TAPBPRØG30L, while both TAPBPRL30G and TAPBPRØloop are least efficient
source: As observed above with HLA-A*68:02, we found that TAPBPRWT was the most efficient catalyst on both HLA-A*02:01 and H-2Kb, followed by TAPBPRØG30L, while both TAPBPRL30G and TAPBPRØloop were least efficient (Figure 6b and c)
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide exchange assays shown in Figures 6b and 6c

claim: The L30 residue in the K22-D35 loop of human TAPBPR plays a critical role in promoting efficient peptide exchange on HLA-A*68:02, HLA-A2 and H-2Kb
source: Thus, although TAPBPR can still mediate peptide exchange on HLA-A2 and H-2Kb in the absence of the loop to some extent, the L30 residue in the K22-D35 loop of human TAPBPR plays a critical role in promoting efficient peptide exchange on HLA-A*68:02, HLA-A2 and H-2Kb
evidence: This is concluded from the functional data across multiple MHC I molecules

claim: HLA-A*68:01 differs from HLA-A*68:02 by only five amino acids
source: We next tested the role of the TAPBPR loop in catalysing peptide exchange on an MHC I molecule that does not accommodate a hydrophobic residue in its F pocket. In order to only explore the contributing role of the F pocket, with minimal other polymorphisms, we chose HLA-A*68:01, since it only differs from HLA-A*68:02 by five amino acids (Niu et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation

claim: There is a significant impairment in the ability of TAPBPRWT to load peptides onto HLA-A*68:01
source: Strikingly, in contrast to the three MHC I molecules tested previously (which all bind hydrophobic residues in their F pocket), there was a significant impairment in the ability of TAPBPRWT to load peptides onto HLA-A*68:01 (Figure 6b and c)
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide exchange assays shown in Figures 6b and 6c

claim: There is no significant difference in the ability of TAPBPR to exchange peptides on HLA-A*68:01 upon mutation of the loop
source: Moreover, there was no significant difference in the ability of TAPBPR to exchange peptides on HLA-A*68:01 upon mutation of the loop, with the different loop variants all exhibiting a similar ability as soluble TAPBPRWT to load the fluorescent peptide KTGGPIYK*R onto HLA-A*68:01 expressed on HeLaM-HLA-ABCKO cells (Figure 6b and c)
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide exchange assays shown in Figures 6b and 6c

claim: HLA-A*68:01 is significantly less responsive to TAPBPR-mediated peptide exchange, which only occurs in a loop-independent manner
source: Thus, in contrast to HLA-A*68:02, which is extremely receptive to TAPBPR-mediated peptide exchange in a loop-dependent manner, HLA-A*68:01 is significantly less responsive to TAPBPR-mediated peptide exchange, which only occurs in a loop-independent manner
evidence: This is concluded from the functional data comparing HLA-A*68:02 and HLA-A*68:01

claim: The five amino acid differences between HLA-A*68:02 and HLA-A*68:01 strongly influence the receptivity of these two MHC I molecules to TAPBPR-mediated peptide exchange
source: Therefore, the five amino acid differences between these two HLA molecules, three of which are around the F pocket (Figure 6d), strongly influence the receptivity of these two MHC I molecules to TAPBPR-mediated peptide exchange, the efficiency of which appears to be strongly influenced by the ability of the K22-D35 loop (specifically L30) to interact with the peptide binding groove
evidence: This is concluded from the functional data and structural analysis

claim: The L30 residue of TAPBPR is capable of binding into the F pocket of MHC I in order promote the dissociation of the bound peptide in a competitive manner
source: These findings support the concept that the L30 residue of TAPBPR is capable of binding into the F pocket of MHC I in order promote the dissociation of the bound peptide in a competitive manner
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion based on the functional data

claim: Residue 116 of MHC I is crucial in determining the F pocket specificity for peptide residues
source: One residue that differs between HLA-A*68:02 and -A*68:01 and was reported to be crucial in determining the F pocket specificity of MHC I for peptide residues is the one on position 116 (Sidney et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature

claim: HLA-A*68:02 contains a tyrosine on position 116, whereas HLA-A*68:01 has an aspartate
source: Namely, HLA-A*68:02 contains a tyrosine on position 116, whereas HLA-A*68:01 has an aspartate (Figure 7a)
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7a

claim: D116 of HLA-A*68:01 forms strong dipole interactions with both residue R114 of the groove and with the arginine on position 9 of the peptide
source: As captured in the two structures, D116 of HLA-A*68:01 forms strong dipole interactions with both residue R114 of the groove and with the arginine on position 9 of the peptide, determining a strong preference of the HLA-A*68:01 F pocket for basic anchor residues
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of crystal structures

claim: Y116 of HLA-A*68:02 does not form any interaction with H114, keeping the hydrophobic patches of the F pocket in an open conformation
source: In contrast, residue Y116 of HLA-A*68:02 does not form any interaction with H114, keeping the hydrophobic patches of the F pocket in an open conformation, which allows it to accommodate hydrophobic peptide residues (Figure 7a)
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 7a

claim: The L30 residue of the TAPBPR loop has access to the F pocket of HLA-A*68:02, but not to the one of HLA-A*68:01
source: We believe that this is the reason why the L30 residue of the TAPBPR loop has access to the F pocket of HLA-A*68:02, but not to the one of HLA-A*68:01
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis based on structural and functional data

claim: TAPBPR exhibits extremely low levels of binding to HLA-A*68:02Y116D compared to HLA-A*68:02WT molecules
source: When we tested the ability of soluble TAPBPRWT to bind to cells expressing the HLA-A*68:02 molecules, strikingly, TAPBPR exhibited extremely low levels of binding to HLA-A*68:02Y116D compared to HLA-A*68:02WT molecules (Figure 7c and d)
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry binding assays shown in Figures 7c and 7d

claim: TAPBPR binding to HLA-A*68:01 is significantly enhanced upon mutation of residue 116 from D to Y
source: Conversely, TAPBPR binding to HLA-A*68:01 was significantly enhanced upon mutation of residue 116 from D to Y (Figure 7c and d)
evidence: This is demonstrated by flow cytometry binding assays shown in Figures 7c and 7d

claim: The binding of TAPBPR to MHC I molecules is directly influenced by the architecture of the F pocket
source: Together, these results demonstrate that the binding of TAPBPR to MHC I molecules is directly influenced by the architecture of the F pocket
evidence: This is concluded from the F pocket mutagenesis and binding data

claim: TAPBPRWT efficiently mediates the loading of ETVSK*QSNV onto HLA-A*68:02WT molecules but fails to load this peptide onto HLA-A*68:02Y116D molecules
source: While TAPBPRWT efficiently mediated the loading of ETVSK*QSNV onto HLA-A*68:02WT molecules, it failed to load this peptide onto HLA-A*68:02Y116D molecules (Figure 7e and f)
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide exchange assays shown in Figures 7e and 7f

claim: TAPBPRWT fails to load ETVSK*QSNV onto HLA-A*68:01WT molecules but efficiently loads this peptide onto HLA-A*68:01D116Y
source: Similarly, TAPBPRWT failed to load ETVSK*QSNV onto HLA-A*68:01WT molecules, however, efficiently loaded this peptide onto HLA-A*68:01D116Y (Figure 7e and f)
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide exchange assays shown in Figures 7e and 7f

claim: TAPBPRWT cannot load KTGGPIYK*R onto HLA-A*68:02WT molecules but can efficiently load this peptide onto HLA-A*68:02Y116D
source: Moreover, we found that while TAPBPRWT could not load KTGGPIYK*R onto HLA-A*68:02WT molecules, it could efficiently load this peptide onto HLA-A*68:02Y116D (Figure 7g and h)
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide exchange assays shown in Figures 7g and 7h

claim: HLA-A*68:01WT can bind KTGGPIYK*R in the presence of TAPBPRWT, but no loading of this peptide is observed onto HLA-A*68:01D116Y
source: Likewise, while HLA-A*68:01WT could bind KTGGPIYK*R in the presence of TAPBPRWT, no loading of this peptide was observed onto HLA-A*68:01D116Y (Figure 7g and h)
evidence: This is demonstrated by peptide exchange assays shown in Figures 7g and 7h

claim: The alterations made to residue 116 of the HLA-A68 molecules have altered peptide specificity
source: These results are in keeping with the fact that the alterations made to the F pocket of the HLA-A68 molecules, and more specifically, to residue 116 alone, have altered peptide specificity
evidence: This is concluded from the peptide exchange data with F pocket mutants

claim: TAPBPR is capable of mediating peptide exchange on HLA-A*68:02Y116D and HLA-A*68:01WT despite low levels of TAPBPR binding
